The Anti-Masonic Party. It was an early U.S. third party of the late 1820s and early 1830s, formed in response to public outcry over alleged Masonic privilege and secrecy. Though short-lived, it pioneered the national nominating convention and later merged into the Whig Party, making it a significant precursor to modern party organization.

The party originated in western New York in the late 1820s, emerging from anti-Masonic sentiment triggered by a shocking crime. In 1826, a man named William Morgan was abducted and murdered because his unpublished manuscript criticizing Masonic oaths threatened Masonic secrecy. When local authorities appeared to protect the Masons accused of Morgan's murder, public fury galvanized a political movement against Masonic influence in American law and government.

The Anti-Masonic Party held the first national nominating convention in American history in 1831. This established the institutional practice that would become standard in both major parties. Presidential candidate William Henry Harrison, who also ran as the National Republican and early Whig nominee, won significant support in 1832, appealing to voters hostile to perceived aristocratic secret societies.

The party's success lay in its focus on secret societies as threats to democratic transparency. It aligned with broader Jacksonian-era suspicion of elite privilege and backroom dealing. But by the mid-1830s, most Anti-Masonic voters migrated to the new Whig Party, which offered a broader anti-Jackson coalition. The Anti-Masonic Party dissolved as a distinct entity by 1840, though its impact on American political institutions—particularly the national nominating convention—persisted long afterward.
